title: GMAT Focus Verbal Practice Test 3
instructions: Original exam-style practice test with answers and explanations.

questions.prompt: Since the Meadowvale bus operator introduced real-time arrival displays at its stops last year, the proportion of passengers reporting satisfaction with punctuality has risen sharply. The operator concludes that its buses are now running more punctually.
questions.question: Which of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the operator's conclusion?
options: A. The displays were funded partly by the local authority.
B. Recorded arrival times show no change in the proportion of buses arriving within the scheduled window.
C. Some passengers say the displays are difficult to read in bright sunlight.
D. Satisfaction with cleanliness also rose over the same period.
E. The operator added two new routes during the year.
questions.explanation: Objective punctuality is unchanged; what improved is passengers' experience of waiting, which displays affect by removing uncertainty. That is a real benefit but not the conclusion drawn. C would weaken the effect of the displays, not the inference about punctuality.

questions.prompt: A health authority plans to raise vaccination rates among older residents by sending each of them a letter stating the date and time of an appointment already booked in their name, which they may change or cancel.
questions.question: The plan's success depends on which of the following assumptions?
options: A. The vaccine is more effective in older residents than in younger ones.
B. The authority has enough letters to send to every resident.
C. Vaccination is currently available only by appointment.
D. Residents prefer letters to text messages.
E. Residents who receive such letters will not be more likely to cancel than to attend.
questions.explanation: Pre-booking works only if the default is accepted more often than it is refused; if the letters prompt cancellations, uptake need not rise. B, D and E are about circumstances rather than the mechanism, and C is a logistical detail already implied.

questions.prompt: A distribution company installed robots to move goods within its warehouse and reports that orders are now picked in less time. A rival argues that the robots cannot be responsible, because the company also reorganised its shelving in the same month.
questions.question: Which of the following, if true, most undermines the rival's argument?
options: A. Picking times fell at the company's other site, where identical robots were installed but the shelving was left unchanged.
B. The reorganisation of shelving was designed by the same consultants who supplied the robots.
C. The company's staff received training on the new system.
D. Order volumes were stable throughout the month.
E. Robots are widely used in comparable warehouses.
questions.explanation: A second site isolates the variable: robots present, shelving unchanged, effect still observed. D removes a different confounder; E is precedent, not evidence about this case.

questions.prompt: Every fishing vessel licensed in the Bardsea district that lands more than fifty tonnes a year is fitted with a satellite tracker. No vessel without a tracker is permitted to fish in the offshore zone. Some vessels licensed in the district land fewer than fifty tonnes a year.
questions.question: If the statements above are true, which of the following must be true?
options: A. Some licensed vessels in the district are not permitted to fish in the offshore zone.
B. Every vessel fishing in the offshore zone lands more than fifty tonnes a year.
C. Any licensed vessel in the district that fishes in the offshore zone has a tracker.
D. Most vessels in the district land fewer than fifty tonnes a year.
E. Vessels without trackers land less than vessels with them.
questions.explanation: The offshore rule requires a tracker of anything fishing there, so a vessel fishing offshore must have one. A does not follow: a small-landing vessel may be fitted with a tracker voluntarily. B reverses the conditional.

questions.prompt: A city is considering removing the entry charge at its municipal museum in order to broaden the range of people who visit.
questions.question: Which of the following would be most useful to determine in evaluating whether the plan will achieve its aim?
options: A. Whether the museum's collection is of national importance
B. How much revenue the charge currently raises
C. Whether other museums in the region charge for entry
D. Whether the charge is the main deterrent for the groups currently under-represented among visitors
E. How many people visited the museum last year
questions.explanation: The aim is a change in the mix of visitors, so what matters is whether price is what keeps the missing groups away — if the deterrents are travel, opening hours or a sense that the place is not for them, free entry will mainly increase visits by people who already came. C matters to affordability, not to the aim.

questions.prompt: A school district found that teachers who had taken part in its mentoring scheme were more likely to remain in post after five years than teachers who had not. The district concluded that mentoring improves retention.
questions.question: The reasoning is most vulnerable to the criticism that it
options: A. assumes that retention is the only measure of a successful scheme
B. overlooks the possibility that teachers who intended to stay were the ones who volunteered for mentoring
C. fails to consider the cost of the scheme
D. relies on data from a single district
E. does not specify how long the mentoring lasted
questions.explanation: Self-selection: commitment to staying may cause participation rather than the reverse. C and D are limitations that do not bear on the causal inference; A misstates the conclusion.

questions.prompt: Insurers now offer lower premiums to drivers who accept a device recording their speed and braking. Since the scheme began, drivers enrolled in it have had markedly fewer accidents than drivers on standard policies, and the insurer attributes this to the effect of monitoring on driving behaviour.
questions.question: Which of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the insurer's attribution?
options: A. The devices also record the time of day at which journeys are made.
B. Premiums for standard policies rose slightly over the same period.
C. Drivers who expect to be judged harshly by such a device are unlikely to enrol in the scheme.
D. Some enrolled drivers disable the device on long journeys.
E. The insurer's accident data are compiled quarterly.
questions.explanation: Enrolment is self-selecting in exactly the relevant respect: careful drivers opt in, so the group would have had fewer accidents without any behavioural effect. D would dilute the effect but does not explain the gap.

questions.prompt: A supermarket introduced labels showing the carbon footprint of each product. Sales of the lowest-footprint items did not rise, although surveys showed that most customers noticed the labels and said they cared about the issue.
questions.question: Which of the following, if true, best explains this outcome?
options: A. The labels were printed in a small typeface.
B. Some customers do not trust footprint figures published by retailers.
C. The supermarket advertised the labels widely.
D. Competing supermarkets introduced similar labels later.
E. The lowest-footprint items were, in most categories, also the items customers were already buying most.
questions.explanation: If the low-footprint items were already the bestsellers, there was little room for the labels to shift sales toward them — the outcome is consistent with the labels working. C would explain indifference but conflicts with customers saying they care.

questions.prompt: An energy consultancy argues that installing rooftop solar panels on a warehouse will reduce the warehouse operator's electricity bill, since the panels will generate a substantial share of the electricity the building uses over a year.
questions.question: The argument depends on which of the following assumptions?
options: A. The panels will require no maintenance during their lifetime.
B. The cost of panels will not fall further in the next few years.
C. The warehouse roof faces south.
D. The building's electricity use is not concentrated in periods when the panels generate little power, in a market where the operator cannot benefit from exporting the surplus.
E. Electricity prices will rise over the life of the panels.
questions.explanation: Annual generation is a total; a bill depends on matching generation to consumption or being paid for exports. The argument fails if the building draws power at night with no export value. D is one way of achieving output but not what the argument requires.

questions.prompt: Opponents of a proposed tax on sugary drinks argue that it will fall hardest on households with the lowest incomes, who spend a larger share of their income on such drinks. Supporters reply that these households also suffer the highest rates of the illnesses the tax is intended to reduce, and would gain most from consuming less.
questions.question: The supporters' reply is best described as
options: A. conceding the opponents' factual claim while disputing what follows from it
B. denying that the tax will affect consumption
C. questioning the accuracy of the opponents' expenditure data
D. shifting the discussion to a different tax
E. arguing that the opponents have a financial interest in the outcome
questions.explanation: The reply accepts that the burden is concentrated and argues that the benefit is concentrated in the same households — a disagreement about the implication, not the fact.

questions.prompt: A publisher observed that its titles with illustrated covers sold better than those with typographic covers, and instructed its designers to use illustrated covers for all future titles.
questions.question: Which of the following, if true, casts most doubt on the wisdom of this instruction?
options: A. Illustrated covers cost more to produce than typographic ones.
B. The publisher's illustrated covers had been used almost exclusively on fiction, which outsells its non-fiction list by a wide margin.
C. Some readers say they prefer typographic covers.
D. Competing publishers use both styles.
E. The publisher's sales rose overall during the period studied.
questions.explanation: The comparison confounds cover style with genre: the sales difference may be fiction outselling non-fiction, in which case applying illustration to non-fiction changes nothing. A bears on cost, not on the sales premise.

questions.passageText:
When several bidders compete for something of uncertain but common value — an oil tract, a broadcasting licence, a company — the winner is by construction the bidder whose estimate of that value was highest. If estimates are distributed around the true value with error, the highest estimate is likely to be an overestimate, and the prize therefore tends to go to the bidder who was most mistaken. This is the winner's curse, and it is a statistical property of the auction rather than a failure of intelligence.

The remedy is counter-intuitive: a rational bidder should shade a bid downward not because the asset is worth less than estimated, but because winning is itself informative. Winning means that every other bidder valued the asset lower, and a bid should be constructed to remain sensible conditional on that news.

Evidence that experienced bidders learn this is mixed. In petroleum lease auctions, returns on tracts sold in the early period of competitive bidding were poor in ways consistent with the curse, and bidding behaviour subsequently became more conservative. In corporate acquisitions the pattern has proved more durable, and the reason may be structural: managers who bid are spending shareholders' money, are rewarded for growth in the size of the firm, and rarely bid often enough to learn from their own losses.

The concept has a boundary that is often ignored. It applies where value is common to all bidders. Where bidders genuinely value the object differently — a house near one buyer's workplace, a patent complementary to one firm's existing portfolio — a high bid may reflect a high private value rather than an error, and the curse does not follow.
questions.prompt: The passage indicates that the winner's curse arises because
options: A. bidders are typically inexperienced in valuing complex assets
B. auctions attract bidders who are willing to take excessive risks
C. sellers withhold information about the asset's true value
D. the bidder with the highest estimate wins, and the highest estimate is likely to be too high
E. the number of bidders in most auctions is too small
questions.explanation: The passage calls it a statistical property of the auction: the winner is by construction the highest estimator, and the highest of a set of error-prone estimates tends to exceed the truth. A and C attribute it to bidder character, which the passage explicitly denies.

questions.explanation: The passage names three structural features: spending shareholders' money, reward for growth in firm size, and too few bids to learn from losses.

questions.passageTitle: Fungal Networks and the Limits of a Metaphor
questions.passageText:
Most land plants form partnerships with fungi at their roots, exchanging sugars for water and mineral nutrients. Since the 1990s a further claim has circulated widely: that these fungi link neighbouring trees into networks through which resources and even warning signals pass, forming what popular accounts call a forest-wide web.

The underlying observations are real. Isotopically labelled carbon applied to one tree has been detected in a neighbour, and fungal strands have been shown to connect the roots of different individuals. The disputed step is interpretive. Detection of transferred carbon does not establish that the quantity is ecologically meaningful, that it travelled through the fungal link rather than through soil after leaf fall or root exudation, or that it moved in a direction that benefits the receiving tree rather than the fungus.

Recent reviews have been pointed. Several found that widely repeated claims — that mature trees preferentially feed their own seedlings, that networks distribute resources to the needy — trace back to a small number of studies whose findings were weaker or more qualified than the citing literature suggests. The fungus, moreover, is not a neutral pipe. It is an organism under selection, and a link between two trees is at least as plausibly a route by which a fungus manages its own supply as a channel of arboreal generosity.

The dispute is instructive about how a metaphor can outrun its evidence. Nothing here shows the networks are unimportant; what is contested is a specific set of functional claims that entered public understanding as settled before they were established.
questions.prompt: The primary purpose of the passage is to
options: A. establish that fungal networks play no significant role in forests
B. describe the mechanism by which fungi exchange nutrients with roots
C. distinguish the observations that are secure from the functional claims that are disputed
D. criticise the researchers who first labelled carbon in forest trees
E. argue that popular science writing should be more technical
questions.explanation: The passage grants the observations, isolates the interpretive step, and closes by saying what is contested is a specific set of functional claims. A overstates: the passage explicitly says nothing shows the networks are unimportant.

questions.prompt: Which of the following, if true, would most strengthen the sceptical position described in the passage?
options: A. Labelled carbon has been detected in neighbouring trees at several sites.
B. Fungal strands connecting different individuals have been photographed.
C. Mature trees in some forests grow faster than nearby seedlings.
D. In experiments where fungal links were severed but soil contact retained, transfer between trees continued at similar levels.
E. Some fungal species associate with only one tree species.
questions.explanation: It attacks the specific inference the sceptics target — that the transfer travels through the fungal link — by showing transfer persists without it. A and B support the observations both sides accept.

questions.passageText:
A price index is meant to answer a simple question: how much more does it cost to be as well off this year as last? The difficulty is that the goods do not stay still.

Consider a laptop that costs the same as last year's model but is substantially faster. A naive index records no change; a hedonic adjustment attributes part of the price to the improved characteristics and records a fall in quality-adjusted price. Statistical agencies use such adjustments extensively, and they matter: because many government payments and contracts are indexed, a persistent bias of even a fraction of a percentage point compounds into large sums.

Critics of the adjustments make two distinct objections that are frequently conflated. The first is technical — that the regressions attributing value to characteristics are sensitive to specification. The second is conceptual and more interesting: a faster processor is a benefit only insofar as it serves purposes people have, and if software expands to consume the additional speed, the user may be no better off while the index records improvement.

There is a symmetrical problem the critics rarely mention. Indices are also slow to capture genuinely new goods, which typically enter after their prices have fallen steeply, so the largest gains occur before the item is measured at all. This bias runs opposite to the one alleged. The honest summary is that the direction of the net error is contested, and that a measurement built on a question about welfare cannot be settled by arithmetic alone.
questions.prompt: The passage suggests that hedonic adjustments matter in practice mainly because
options: A. consumers are unaware of quality improvements in the goods they buy
B. statistical agencies disagree about how to define a laptop
C. many payments and contracts are indexed, so small persistent biases compound
D. new goods are introduced more rapidly than in the past
E. manufacturers change model numbers frequently
questions.explanation: Stated directly: indexation means a fraction of a percentage point compounds into large sums.

options: A. an improvement counts as a benefit only if it serves purposes people actually have
B. the regressions used are sensitive to specification
C. quality improvements are impossible to quantify
D. agencies adjust prices downward more readily than upward

options: A. show that the critics' concerns apply to a wider class of products

questions.passageText:
The technique of recording each transaction twice, as a debit in one account and a credit in another, was described in print by Luca Pacioli in 1494, though merchants in northern Italy had used it for two centuries before. Its historical significance has been both overstated and underappreciated, in different respects.

The overstatement is causal. Some accounts present double entry as a precondition of capitalism, on the argument that rational calculation of profit made systematic investment possible. The chronology is unhelpful to this claim: the method spread slowly, many large and successful enterprises kept single-entry records well into the nineteenth century, and its adoption often followed rather than preceded commercial expansion.

The underappreciated contribution is narrower and more durable. Double entry makes a firm's accounts internally checkable. Because every entry appears twice with opposite signs, the books can be tested for consistency without reference to anything outside them, which permits errors to be located and makes certain frauds harder to conceal. It also separates the firm's affairs from those of its owner — an abstraction that had to be invented, and without which the idea of a company as an entity that can own, owe and be audited is difficult to formulate.

That is the more defensible claim. Double entry was not the engine of commercial growth; it was an instrument for making an enterprise legible to people who did not run it, and that capacity became indispensable exactly when firms grew too large for their owners to observe directly.
questions.prompt: The passage argues that the claim that double-entry bookkeeping was a precondition of capitalism is weakened primarily by
options: A. evidence that Pacioli did not invent the method
B. the chronology of the method's adoption
C. the existence of alternative accounting techniques in Asia
D. the difficulty of defining capitalism precisely
E. the fact that most merchants were illiterate
questions.explanation: The passage says the method spread slowly, large firms used single entry into the nineteenth century, and adoption often followed commercial expansion.

options: A. a decisive cause of commercial expansion
B. a minor technical refinement of little consequence

Evidence that experienced bidders learn this is mixed. In petroleum lease auctions, returns on tracts sold in the early period of competitive bidding were poor in ways consistent with the curse, and bidding behaviour subsequently became more conservative. In corporate acquisitions the pattern has proved more durable, and the reason may be structural: managers who bid are spending shareholders' money, are rewarded for growth in the size of the firm, and rarely bid often enough to learn from their own losses.

The concept has a boundary that is often ignored. It applies where value is common to all bidders. Where bidders genuinely value the object differently — a house near one buyer's workplace, a patent complementary to one firm's existing portfolio — a high bid may reflect a high private value rather than an error, and the curse does not follow.

readingPassages.title: Fungal Networks and the Limits of a Metaphor
readingPassages.text:
Most land plants form partnerships with fungi at their roots, exchanging sugars for water and mineral nutrients. Since the 1990s a further claim has circulated widely: that these fungi link neighbouring trees into networks through which resources and even warning signals pass, forming what popular accounts call a forest-wide web.

The underlying observations are real. Isotopically labelled carbon applied to one tree has been detected in a neighbour, and fungal strands have been shown to connect the roots of different individuals. The disputed step is interpretive. Detection of transferred carbon does not establish that the quantity is ecologically meaningful, that it travelled through the fungal link rather than through soil after leaf fall or root exudation, or that it moved in a direction that benefits the receiving tree rather than the fungus.

Recent reviews have been pointed. Several found that widely repeated claims — that mature trees preferentially feed their own seedlings, that networks distribute resources to the needy — trace back to a small number of studies whose findings were weaker or more qualified than the citing literature suggests. The fungus, moreover, is not a neutral pipe. It is an organism under selection, and a link between two trees is at least as plausibly a route by which a fungus manages its own supply as a channel of arboreal generosity.

The dispute is instructive about how a metaphor can outrun its evidence. Nothing here shows the networks are unimportant; what is contested is a specific set of functional claims that entered public understanding as settled before they were established.

readingPassages.title: Measuring the Cost of Living
readingPassages.text:
A price index is meant to answer a simple question: how much more does it cost to be as well off this year as last? The difficulty is that the goods do not stay still.

Consider a laptop that costs the same as last year's model but is substantially faster. A naive index records no change; a hedonic adjustment attributes part of the price to the improved characteristics and records a fall in quality-adjusted price. Statistical agencies use such adjustments extensively, and they matter: because many government payments and contracts are indexed, a persistent bias of even a fraction of a percentage point compounds into large sums.

Critics of the adjustments make two distinct objections that are frequently conflated. The first is technical — that the regressions attributing value to characteristics are sensitive to specification. The second is conceptual and more interesting: a faster processor is a benefit only insofar as it serves purposes people have, and if software expands to consume the additional speed, the user may be no better off while the index records improvement.

There is a symmetrical problem the critics rarely mention. Indices are also slow to capture genuinely new goods, which typically enter after their prices have fallen steeply, so the largest gains occur before the item is measured at all. This bias runs opposite to the one alleged. The honest summary is that the direction of the net error is contested, and that a measurement built on a question about welfare cannot be settled by arithmetic alone.

readingPassages.title: Double-Entry Bookkeeping
readingPassages.text:
The technique of recording each transaction twice, as a debit in one account and a credit in another, was described in print by Luca Pacioli in 1494, though merchants in northern Italy had used it for two centuries before. Its historical significance has been both overstated and underappreciated, in different respects.

The overstatement is causal. Some accounts present double entry as a precondition of capitalism, on the argument that rational calculation of profit made systematic investment possible. The chronology is unhelpful to this claim: the method spread slowly, many large and successful enterprises kept single-entry records well into the nineteenth century, and its adoption often followed rather than preceded commercial expansion.

The underappreciated contribution is narrower and more durable. Double entry makes a firm's accounts internally checkable. Because every entry appears twice with opposite signs, the books can be tested for consistency without reference to anything outside them, which permits errors to be located and makes certain frauds harder to conceal. It also separates the firm's affairs from those of its owner — an abstraction that had to be invented, and without which the idea of a company as an entity that can own, owe and be audited is difficult to formulate.

That is the more defensible claim. Double entry was not the engine of commercial growth; it was an instrument for making an enterprise legible to people who did not run it, and that capacity became indispensable exactly when firms grew too large for their owners to observe directly.
